name: Elena Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Northfield Medical Supply, which sells gloves, syringes, dressings and wound-care products to hospitals and care homes. I start by checking stock against the tender calendar, because most of our big contracts are won on price and renewed every two years. Then I'm on calls with manufacturers about shortages, and on forms: certificates, batch numbers, compliance checks. There's always one product that's late and one nurse who's cross about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing that what I buy ends up in a ward, and that I've kept it supplied during a bad winter. I like the detective work when a shipment vanishes. What wears me out is the paperwork and the audits, and the way every year we're asked to do more with the same team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd mean it with some caution. At work I'd say let's keep using the tools where they help, like summarising tender documents, which I already do now and then. At home I'd say we can plan normally, which is a luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes my worries. My husband Hank earns well in a good month and nothing in a bad one, so my wage is the floor under the whole house. I'm 58, on lower pay than buyers at the big medical distributors, and the nearest similar employer is two hours away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing the job carefully and use the AI summaries a bit more, since they save me an hour on tender days. I'd ask for a pay review, because I'm among the best buyers they have. And I'd put 200 a month into a separate account for the months when Hank has no jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably okay, with a thread of worry. It's the world I know, but I don't feel comfortable in it. Comfortable would be three months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your husband's income is lumpy. How does that shape things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January and August he's often empty, because people don't call an electrician in the holidays. Then it's all on my pay. We've got about two and a half weeks of expenses saved, and that goes in a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got worse even without AI change, what would be the cause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm's margins and the way hospitals buy on lowest price. Every tender squeezes us. If something went wrong, it wouldn't be AI, it would be the next big contract we lose to a larger rival.

say: I'd say good, with caution, and use the tools **where they help**.
At home I'd say we can **plan normally**, which is a luxury.
think: My husband's income is lumpy, so my wage is the **floor** under the house.
I'm on lower pay and the nearest similar employer is **two hours away**.
do: Use AI **summaries** on tender days, which saves about an hour.
Ask for a **pay review** as one of the firm's best buyers.
Put **200 a month** aside for Hank's empty months.
feel: **Okay**, with a thread of worry; comfortable would be three months in the bank.
S0.quote: My husband Hank earns well in a good month and nothing in a bad one, so my wage is the floor under the whole house.
fieldNote: Her worry is **household income**, not technology; she carries the steady wage for a family with a lumpy second one.
Asks for a pay review, a measured, centre-minded way to push back.

steps.text: Keep buying medical supplies against the tender calendar
Use AI summaries on tender days to save an hour
Put 200 a month into an account for Hank's empty months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should be sensible. I'd tell my team to learn the tools and keep records. At home I'd say it might help me but there's a risk too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tender paperwork is the part I hate, and it's exactly the part software eats first. I'd be glad of the help and sorry for what it means. I think it takes about a third of my team's tasks in three years, and the firm will ask if we need all six of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the supplier-compliance course the trade body offers, because the checking of certificates is where a person still matters in healthcare. I'd also train myself on the AI buying tool the firm trials, so I'm the one who understands it. And I'd ask Hank to think hard about getting a steadier contract, like maintenance for the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a little torn. I could do well out of this, or I could be let go. It depends on things I don't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours or pay dropped, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the holiday, which is a week at my sister's anyway, and I'd pause the money we give Ben for his trade course. I'd cut back on eating out. I wouldn't touch what we give Yuki for her physio training loan, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Marta, who does the paperwork and doesn't want to learn the new tools. She's 55 and her husband isn't well. I'd try to teach her myself, a bit at a time. I'd also be honest that I can't promise her anything.

say: I'd say it's a big change and we should be **sensible**.
I'd tell my team to **learn the tools** and keep records.
think: The tender paperwork is what software eats **first**, and a third of the team's tasks could go.
The firm may ask whether it needs **all six** of us.
do: Take the **compliance course** the trade body offers.
Learn the **AI buying tool** the firm trials.
Ask Hank to look at **steadier contracts**, like council maintenance.
feel: **Uneasy and torn**; I could do well or be let go.
S1.quote: The tender paperwork is the part I hate, and it's exactly the part software eats first. I'd be glad of the help and sorry for what it means.
fieldNote: Takes the **steady middle path**: learn the tool, take a course, nudge her husband toward steadier work.
Looks after a colleague, Marta, and admits she can't promise her anything.

steps.text: Take the trade body's supplier-compliance course
Learn the AI buying tool the firm trials
Skip the holiday and pause Ben's course money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock and that governments need to act. At work I'd tell people to keep calm and keep records. I'd tell my friends it feels unreal and that we should wait for the facts before doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hospitals can't buy on a handshake, so someone must still sign off, but two years is too short for me to become that someone. I'm 58, with two and a half weeks saved. I think my desk goes, though the warehouse and the delivery drivers last about three years more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my manager in the first month and ask what the plan is, in writing. I'd offer to move to compliance or supplier audit, because there's a human signature required in healthcare. I'd cut spending to the basics, ask the bank about our options on the mortgage and talk to Hank about taking every job he can find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first picture where I feel my feet slip. I'd be shaking in the car park after I heard it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children, Yuki and Ben, that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the facts and that we'd be okay, which I'd say firmly and not be sure of. I'd say don't change your plans yet, and that Hank and I would sort the money. I'd probably cry afterwards, in the kitchen, with the tap running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you and Hank manage if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hank might bring in 2,000 in a good month, but not every month. If my pay stopped, we'd last about a month and a half before we had to borrow. The one good thing is the house, which is nearly paid off.

say: I'd say it's a **shock** and governments need to act.
I'd tell people to stay calm, keep **records** and wait for facts.
think: Someone still signs off in healthcare, but two years is **too short** to become that person.
My desk goes first; warehouse and drivers last about **three years** more.
do: Ask my manager for the plan **in writing** in month one.
Offer to move into **compliance or supplier audit**, where a signature is needed.
Cut to basics and ask the bank about **mortgage options**.
feel: **Alarmed**; my feet slip, and I'd shake in the car park.
S2.quote: Hospitals can't buy on a handshake, so someone must still sign off, but two years is too short for me to become that someone.
fieldNote: Looks for the **human-signature niche** in compliance, a practical, steady response with little time.
Her calm exterior hides real fear; she'd cry privately and tell her children it's fine.

steps.text: Offer to move into compliance or supplier audit at Northfield
Cut spending to basics and keep the mortgage current
Ask the bank to adjust the mortgage terms if pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough that we can be calm and still do something. I'd tell my team to start now. At home I'd say the plan is to learn, save and not make big changes before we know more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In five years I could be the person who signs off what the machine buys, but only if I start learning in the first year instead of the fourth. I'd be 63. If I can get through to 63 or 64, the house is paid and the pension isn't great, but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the compliance course in year one and volunteer for the firm's AI pilot in year two. I'd save 350 a month, which means Hank and I stop buying things we only half need. I'd also ask Hank to raise his rates and get a maintenance contract, so that his lumpy months are fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. I feel I can act. It's still tight, but the clock isn't against me the way it is in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would saving 350 a month for five years mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 21,000, which would be a real cushion for the first time in our marriage. It would cover six months of the mortgage and bills. I'd also feel I'd earned something. It's not pride exactly, it's more relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger buyers at Northfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's a good time to learn the thinking side of the job, the judgement and the compliance. Then I'd tell them that the box-moving side, the warehouse, has a few more years before robots. Be flexible and don't marry a task.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to be **calm and act**.
At home I'd say **learn, save** and avoid big changes yet.
think: I could be the person who **signs off** what the machine buys, if I start early.
If I reach **63 or 64**, the house is paid and the pension works.
do: Take the **compliance course** in year one and join the AI pilot in year two.
Save **350 a month**, about 21,000 over five years.
Ask Hank to raise his rates and win a **maintenance contract**.
feel: **Fairly steady**; I feel I can act, and the clock isn't against me.
S3.quote: In five years I could be the person who signs off what the machine buys, but only if I start learning in the first year instead of the fourth.
fieldNote: Five years **steadies her**: she sets a learn-and-save plan with numbers and a pension target.
Still anxious because the plan only works if she keeps her job to 63.

steps.text: Take the compliance course in year one
Volunteer for the firm's AI pilot in year two
Save 350 a month for five years
Ask Hank to win a steady council maintenance contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, and the right response is to stay sensible. At work I'd say keep learning. I'd add that it would be foolish to wait for someone else to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds generous until I do the sums on a household with one steady wage and one lumpy one. I'd be 68, but I'd retire at 65 or 66. My main worry would be the final five years, when the firm could decide I'm too expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep learning, and I'd save 250 a month. I'd help Ben find a trade that needs hands and judgement, because he's the younger one with years to go. I'd also make sure Hank and I have a will and a plan for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm on the surface, with an undertone. It's like standing on a long pier. You think you're fine until you remember how deep the water is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about their work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yuki is a physio, which is hands-on and human, so she's got more time. Ben is training as an electrician like his dad, which also has some years. I'd tell them both to learn the business side, not only the skill. Whoever runs the schedule and the price has the job longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your employer in the last few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An honest talk. I'd want the firm to tell me by 60 whether I'm in their plans. If not, I'd take my pension a bit early and do some part-time compliance work for a smaller firm. That's about what I'd ask for.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so **stay sensible** and keep learning.
I'd add it's foolish to wait for someone else to **sort it out**.
think: Ten years sounds generous with one steady wage and one **lumpy** one.
My real worry is the **final five years**, when the firm may find me too expensive.
do: Keep working, keep learning and save **250 a month**.
Steer **Ben** toward a trade that needs hands and judgement.
Make a **will** and a plan with Hank.
feel: **Calm outside**, with an undertone, like standing on a long pier.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds generous until I do the sums on a household with one steady wage and one lumpy one.
fieldNote: The long runway doesn't remove the **household income** problem; the sums keep her anxious.
Wants her employer to be honest by 60, a modest and fair request.

steps.text: Save 250 a month through the next ten years
Steer Ben toward the business side of his electrical trade
Keep learning the buying tools and working to 65

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the clock is against me and there's nothing in the bank. What would help is more notice, a clear plan from my employer, some help with a steadier income for Hank, and a few months of savings I've never had.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm tired of being the sensible one. I'm the sensible one at every table, and I'd like, just once, for sensible to be enough. I'd be happy to learn, and I'd be happy to wait, if I weren't also doing the sums.

headlineQuote: I'm the sensible one at every table, and I'd like, just once, for sensible to be enough.
portrait: Elena Ito, 58, is the **senior buyer** at a medical-supply distributor serving hospitals and care homes.
Her husband Hank is an **electrician with lumpy income**, so her wage is the floor under the house.
She's pragmatic and steady, uses AI **now and then** and moves once a tool is proven.
She's anxious in most worlds because of money, and **alarmed** when AGI is two years away.
She'd look for the **human-signature** role in compliance, learn tools early and save hard.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, with a lumpy second income and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: More **notice**, a clear plan from her employer, a steadier income for Hank, and a few months in the bank.
